newsitem.title: PORTUGAL: Russia defends Milosevic at summit, sources say.
newsitem.headline: Russia defends Milosevic at summit, sources say.

text.p: Russia defended Serbian President Slobodan Milosevic at a European security summit on Tuesday, insisting on striking out a call for Serbian democracy from a final declaration, Western diplomatic sources said.

A draft of the final communique of the Organisation for Security and Cooperation in Europe (OSCE) summit, due to be issued on Tuesday, made clear that the meeting believed democracy, an independent media and free elections in Yugoslavia were vital to stability in the Balkans.
Overnight the sentence -- "Democratisation, independent media, free and fair elections are critical to fostering lasting stability in the area" -- disappeared from a later draft.
"The Russians have been insistent and eloquent defenders of the unfortunate Yugoslav position," a Western diplomatic source said.

The change would considerably tone down any criticism of Belgrade from the summit at a time when opposition and student demonstrators were on the streets in the biggest protest against Milosevic's nine-year rule.
International peace coordinator Carl Bildt joined Britain and France on Monday to express "deep concern" over a government threat to crack down on the two weeks of protests.
The draft of the final communique merely says that the OSCE should involve itself in accelerating democratisation, promoting an independent media and ensuring free elections.
Yugoslavia -- comprising Serbia and Montenegro -- was suspended from the OSCE body in 1992 after being accused of stoking the war in neighbouring Bosnia.
Russia wants Yugoslavia to be readmitted to the organisation following the Dayton agreement that ended the 43-month war in Bosnia and the lifting of most sanctions against Belgrade.

Many OSCE nations, including Bosnia, Croatia and Slovenia, insist Yugoslavia must reapply for membership to the body, arguing it is no longer the same country as before, a position Belgrade dismisses.
The question of succession is also complicating talks on the resolution of former Yugoslavia's debts and assets among the former Yugoslav republics.
